title: Rate of Change
text:
Goal
The goal of this lecture is to understand the derivative as a mathematical tool for measuring instantaneous rate of change.

title: Rate of Change
Rate of Change
text:
Average rate of change
Suppose \(y = f(x)\). The average rate of change of \(f\) from \(x = a\) to \(x = b\) is
\[
\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}.
\]
Geometrically, this is the slope of the secant line connecting the two points
\[
(a, f(a))
\quad \text{and} \quad
(b, f(b)).
\]
The average rate of change measures how much the function changes over an interval.

title: Rate of Change
text:
Instantaneous rate of change
To define the instantaneous rate of change at \(x = a\), we let \(b\) move closer and closer to \(a\).
Equivalently, write
\[
b = a + h.
\]
Then the average rate of change becomes
\[
\frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}.
\]
The derivative is defined as the limit
\[
f'(a)
=
\lim_{h \to 0}
\frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h},
\]
provided this limit exists.

title: Rate of Change
Rate of Change
text:
Example
Let
\[
f(x) = x^2.
\]
Then
\[
f'(a)
=
\lim_{h \to 0}
\frac{(a+h)^2 - a^2}{h}.
\]
Expand the numerator:
\[
(a+h)^2 - a^2
=
a^2 + 2ah + h^2 - a^2
=
2ah + h^2.
\]
Therefore,
\[
f'(a)
=
\lim_{h \to 0}
\frac{2ah + h^2}{h}.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{2ah + h^2}{h}
=
2a + h,
\]
we have
\[
f'(a)
=
\lim_{h \to 0}
(2a + h)
=
2a.
\]
So if \(f(x) = x^2\), then
\[
f'(x) = 2x.
\]

title: Rate of Change
text:
Statistical connection
This idea appears often in statistics.
For example, if \(\ell(\theta)\) is a log-likelihood function, then the derivative
\[
\frac{d}{d\theta}\ell(\theta)
\]
measures how fast the log-likelihood changes as the parameter \(\theta\) changes.
The maximum likelihood estimator often satisfies the score equation
\[
\frac{d}{d\theta}\ell(\theta) = 0.
\]
So understanding derivatives is foundational for likelihood theory, optimization, regression, and asymptotic statistics.

title: Rate of Change
text:
Key takeaway
A derivative is the limit of average rates of change. It measures the instantaneous rate of change of a function and gives the slope of the tangent line.

title: Lecture 7 (DESeq; p-values; supervised learning; K-means)
text:
Clustering

Notation
Data: \(\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n\), \(i = 1,\ldots,n\), where \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is a \(p \times 1\) column vector.
Let \(c_i\) denote the membership of \(\mathbf{x}_i\) belonging to one of the K clusters.


Euclidean Distance

\(\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_{i^{\prime}}\|_F = d(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_{i^{\prime}}) = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^p \left(x_{ij} - x_{i^{\prime}j}\right)^2}\)
Also known as \(l_2\)-norm



K-means Clustering

K-means clustering is applicable to Euclidean distance.
The goal is to find \(K\) centers, denoted by \(\mathbf{m}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{m}_K \in \mathbb{R}^p\), that minimizes \[\sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{i: c_i = k} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{m}_k\|_F^2 = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{i: c_i = k}\sum_{j=1}^p (x_{ij} - m_{kj})^2 = f\left(\{c_i\}_{i=1}^n, \{\mathbf{m}_k\}_{k=1}^K\right). \tag{1}\]
K-means clustering is guaranteed to converge to a local minimum of the objective function (1).
K-means clustering does not work when Euclidean distance is not a good measure of dissimilarity, e.g., Swiss roll problem.
For the Swiss roll problem, a solution is to use spectral clustering.
K-means clustering also does not work well when there are outliers.
To check for outliers, we desire to plot data first by dimension reduction.



An Iterative Algorithm
Data points are assigned randomly to one of the K clusters: \(c_1^{(0)}, \ldots, c_n^{(0)}\).
Then, at the \(r\)th interaction, \(r = 1, 2, \ldots\),

we update cluster centers by solving the following minimization problem \[\mathbf{m}_k^{(r)} = \underset{\mathbf{m}_k \in \mathbb{R}^p}{\arg\min} \sum_{i: c_i^{(r-1)} = k} \sum_{j=1}^p (x_{ij} - m_{kj})^2 \implies m_{kj}^{(r)} = \frac{1}{n_k^{(r-1)}}\sum_{i: c_i^{(r-1)} = k}x_{ij}\] (hint: differentiate with respect to \(m_{kj}\)’s for \(j = 1, \ldots, p\).)
we then update cluster assignment by solving the following minimization problem \[c_i^{(r)} = \underset{k=1,\ldots, K}{\arg\min} \left\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{m}_k^{(r)}\right\|_F^2\] (hint: write (1) in an equivalent form by taking the summation of data points of i from 1 to n.)

We stop when \(c_i^{(r)} = c_i^{(r-1)}\) for all i.


The Local Minimum Problem
The iterative algorithm implemented in the K-means clustering works towards minimizing the objective function (1) at each step, and thus almost always leads to a local minimum.
To address this local minimum problem, we can do random initialization multiple times.


Kernel Trick
Intuitively speaking, lower-dimensional data are projected to a higher-dimensional space so that they can be more easily separated?


K-medians

\(l_2\)-norm is changed to \(l_1\)-norm given by \[\|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_{i^{\prime}}\|_1 = \sum_{i=1}^p |x_{ij} - x_{i^{\prime}j}|.\]
It can be shown that the solution to \[
\underset{\mathbf{m}_k \in \mathbb{R}^p}{\arg\min}
\sum_{i: c_i = k}
\left\| \mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{m}_k \right\|_1 = \underset{\mathbf{m}_k \in \mathbb{R}^p}{\arg\min}
\sum_{i: c_i = k} \sum_{i=1}^p |x_{ij} - m_{kj}|
\] is \(m_{kj} = \mathrm{median}(x_{ij})_{i: c_i = k}.\)
